questions.statement: She ___ swim very well because she practises every day. Choose the correct modal.
questions.context: A student knows how to swim very well.

options.feedback: Can expresses ability, and swimming well is the ability this sentence describes.
Must expresses obligation or strong necessity, not the ability to swim.
Should gives advice or a recommendation, not the physical ability to swim.
May expresses possibility or permission, not the ability to swim well.

questions.explanation:
Ability in the present is expressed with can plus the bare infinitive: she can swim. Must, should and may do not describe ability.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: When he was five, he ___ read simple books. Choose the correct modal.
questions.context: When he was five, he already knew how to read.

options.feedback: Can is present, but the sentence places the ability at age five.
Could is the past form of can and reports a general ability in the past.
Must expresses obligation and does not fit a past ability.
Should gives advice and cannot report what he was able to do.

questions.explanation:
Past ability uses could plus the bare infinitive: he could read. Can is present, so it clashes with the past time marker.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ I open the window, please? Choose the correct modal.
questions.context: A student asks the teacher politely for permission to open the window.

options.feedback: Must asks about obligation, not about permission to open a window.
Should asks for advice and does not request permission.
May asks for permission politely, which is exactly what the student wants.
Would is used for offers and hypotheticals, not for asking permission here.

questions.explanation:
May I plus the infinitive is the polite formula for requesting permission. Must, should and would do not ask permission in this context.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Drivers ___ stop at a red light. Choose the correct modal.
questions.context: The law requires drivers to stop at a red light.

options.feedback: Can expresses ability or permission, not a legal requirement.
Might expresses a weak possibility, not an obligation.
Could expresses past ability or possibility, not a rule.
Must expresses a strong obligation, and the law makes the stop obligatory.

questions.explanation:
A legal requirement is a strong obligation, so must is correct. Can, might and could describe ability or possibility, not duty.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She ___ arrive at the office before eight. Choose the correct form.
questions.context: Her office starts at eight, so she needs to arrive early.

options.feedback: Has to agrees with the third person singular she and expresses the external obligation.
Must to is wrong because must never takes to before the infinitive.
Have to is plural and does not agree with the singular subject she.
Should to is wrong because should never takes to before the infinitive.

questions.explanation:
External obligation in the third person singular is has to plus the infinitive: she has to arrive. Must and should take no to.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You ___ pay; the entrance is free. Choose the correct form.
questions.context: It is not necessary to pay, but you may if you wish.

options.feedback: Mustn't means prohibition, but paying is allowed, only unnecessary.
Don't have to means there is no obligation, which matches the free entrance.
Shouldn't gives advice against paying, which is stronger than the idea of free entry.
Can't means it is impossible or not permitted, not merely unnecessary.

questions.explanation:
Absence of obligation is don't have to. Mustn't forbids the action, while here paying is permitted but not required.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You ___ go to bed early tonight. Choose the correct modal.
questions.context: Your friend feels tired and has an important exam tomorrow.

options.feedback: Must states a strong obligation, too forceful for a piece of advice.
May expresses permission or possibility, not a recommendation.
Should gives advice or a recommendation, which fits the friendly suggestion.
Can expresses ability or permission, not advice about sleeping.

questions.explanation:
Advice is normally given with should plus the bare infinitive. Must is stronger and states an obligation rather than a suggestion.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ you pass me the document, please? Choose the correct modal.
questions.context: You want your colleague to pass you a document politely.

options.feedback: Must asks about obligation and sounds like an order, not a request.
May asks for permission and cannot ask someone to pass a document.
Should asks for advice and does not work as a polite request here.
Could makes the request polite and tentative, which suits a colleague.

questions.explanation:
Could you plus the infinitive is a polite request. May asks permission and must states obligation, so neither fits asking a favour.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: It ___ rain this afternoon, so take an umbrella. Choose the correct modal.
questions.context: The sky is grey, so rain is possible later.

options.feedback: May expresses possibility, and a grey sky makes rain possible but not certain.
Must expresses certainty or obligation, but the rain is only possible.
Should expresses advice or expectation, not a simple possibility.
Can expresses ability or general possibility, not a specific forecast.

questions.explanation:
A possible future event is expressed with may plus the bare infinitive: it may rain. Must would state certainty, which the evidence does not support.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Visitors ___ touch the paintings. Choose the correct modal.
questions.context: A museum rule forbids visitors to touch the paintings.

options.feedback: Don't have to means it is unnecessary, but here touching is not allowed.
Mustn't expresses prohibition, and the museum rule forbids touching.
Might not expresses a possibility that something will not happen, not a ban.
Couldn't reports past inability, which does not match a present rule.

questions.explanation:
A ban is expressed with mustn't. Don't have to would mean touching is optional, and might not and couldn't do not forbid anything.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: After the course, you ___ drive a car. Choose the correct form.
questions.context: After the course, you will have the skill to drive.

options.feedback: Will can is wrong because can never follows will directly.
Can is present ability and cannot follow the future marker will.
Will be able to expresses ability in the future, which can does not cover.
Could is past ability or a hypothetical, not a future skill.

questions.explanation:
For future ability, English uses will be able to because can has no future form of its own. Will can is never grammatical.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Last week we ___ work late to finish the project. Choose the correct form.
questions.context: Last week the team worked late because of a deadline.

options.feedback: Must has no past form, so it cannot report last week's obligation.
Have to is present and clashes with the time phrase last week.
Should gives advice and does not report what was obligatory.
Had to is the past form of have to and reports the past obligation.

questions.explanation:
Past obligation is reported with had to. Must lacks a past form, and have to is present, so neither fits last week.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ I watch television now, Mum? Choose the correct modal.
questions.context: A child asks a parent for permission to watch television.

options.feedback: Can asks for permission in an informal way, which suits a child at home.
Must asks about obligation and cannot request permission to watch TV.
Should asks for advice and does not ask for permission.
Would is used in offers and hypotheticals, not in this request.

questions.explanation:
Can I plus the infinitive is the informal way to ask permission. May is more formal, while must, should and would do not request permission.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The train ___ arrive in a few minutes. Choose the correct modal.
questions.context: The train left an hour ago, so it arrives soon.

options.feedback: Must expresses certainty or obligation, but an arrival time is an expectation.
Should expresses a strong expectation based on the schedule, which fits the timing.
Can expresses ability or permission, not a prediction about arrival.
May expresses a weaker possibility, while the schedule supports a firm expectation.

questions.explanation:
Should can express a confident expectation: the train should arrive soon. Must states certainty, which the evidence cannot guarantee.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You ___ take the exam if you do not want to. Choose the correct form.
questions.context: The exam is optional, so nobody is required to take it.

options.feedback: Mustn't forbids taking the exam, but it is allowed and only optional.
Can't says it is impossible or not allowed, which is too strong.
Don't have to states that the exam is optional, which matches the context.
Shouldn't advises against it, but the choice is neutral.

questions.explanation:
Optional actions use don't have to. Mustn't would ban the exam, can't would make it impossible, and shouldn't would advise against it.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You ___ eat less salt for your health. Choose the correct form.
questions.context: A doctor gives a patient a recommendation about salt.

options.feedback: Must states a strong obligation, which is more forceful than medical advice.
Can expresses ability or permission and does not give advice.
May expresses permission or possibility and does not recommend anything.
Ought to expresses advice and is followed by the bare infinitive eat.

questions.explanation:
Advice can be given with ought to plus the infinitive: you ought to eat less salt. Must states obligation, while can and may do not advise.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: That ___ be the postman; he always comes at this time. Choose the correct modal.
questions.context: Someone is knocking at the door, and the family is expecting the postman.

options.feedback: Must expresses a strong deduction, and the regular time makes the postman very likely.
Can't expresses a deduction that something is impossible, the opposite of this evidence.
Should gives advice or expectation, not a logical deduction about who it is.
May expresses weak possibility, but the evidence supports a strong conclusion.

questions.explanation:
Strong logical deduction is expressed with must: that must be the postman. Can't would deny it, and may would only suggest a weak possibility.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: He ___ open the jar, however hard he tried. Choose the correct modal.
questions.context: He tried hard but was unable to open the jar.

options.feedback: Mustn't expresses prohibition, not an inability to open a jar.
Couldn't reports the lack of ability in the past, which matches his failed attempt.
Shouldn't gives advice against the action, not a lack of ability.
Needn't means it was unnecessary, but he tried and failed.

questions.explanation:
Past inability is couldn't plus the bare infinitive: he couldn't open the jar. Mustn't forbids, shouldn't advises, and needn't says something is unnecessary.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Every employee ___ wear a helmet in the factory. Choose the correct modal.
questions.context: A workplace safety rule is compulsory for every employee.

options.feedback: Should only recommends the helmet, but the safety rule is compulsory.
Could expresses possibility or past ability, not a requirement.
Must expresses the compulsory rule that every employee has to follow.
Might expresses a weak possibility, not a safety obligation.

questions.explanation:
A compulsory safety rule requires must. Should would only advise, and could and might describe possibility, not obligation.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You ___ bring a guest to the club; entry is for members only. Choose the correct form.
questions.context: You may enter the club, but bringing a guest is not allowed.

options.feedback: Don't have to means it is optional, but guests are not permitted at all.
Shouldn't gives advice, which is weaker than the club's rule.
Might not expresses a possibility that you will not bring a guest, not a ban.
Mustn't states the prohibition on bringing a guest, which the rule makes clear.

questions.explanation:
A prohibition is mustn't: bringing a guest is forbidden. Don't have to would make it optional, and shouldn't would only advise against it.
---
